reference_reasoning.proposition: The dense basal planar defects seen as fault-like contrast on (0001) and as heavy-atom-rich bright bands only a few layers wide are identified as LPSO nanoplates, aggregates of four-layer Zn/Y-segregated fcc-type stacking faults rather than conventional stacking faults [n8]. Heat treatment is shown to set the nanoplate density and thickness, giving 9.8 per um at ~28 nm as-grown, ~0.3 per um at ~84 nm after 520 C, and ~9.0 per um at ~14 nm after the further 400 C anneal [n9].
reference_reasoning.assumption: The reasoning assumes that the fault-like g=0002 contrast and the heavy-atom-rich HAADF bands both signal the same Zn/Y-segregated four-layer stacking feature rather than unrelated contrast effects, and that the phase identity stays fixed across the three heat-treatment states so that the observed changes in count and thickness reflect coarsening and re-formation of the same LPSO nanoplates rather than a different phase appearing [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.open: The exact atomic stacking registry within the four-layer fault and the physical mechanism (dissolution versus coarsening) that turns the many thin as-grown plates into one thick plate at 520 C before more thin plates return after the 400 C anneal are not established by these images alone [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.handoff: The next step inherits an identified LPSO nanoplate phase whose density and thickness can be tuned by heat treatment across the three states of 9.8 per um / ~28 nm, ~0.3 per um / ~84 nm, and ~9.0 per um / ~14 nm [n9], giving a controllable microstructural feature to relate to subsequent mechanical or anisotropy behavior [n8].

dependency.why: The TEM observations (obs1-4) directly establish the nanoplates' phase identity and their heat-treatment-tunable density and thickness on their own, without requiring any prior step's conclusion as input.

observations: Panel F8a shows yield stress in [11-20] at RT falling from 167 MPa as-grown to 113 MPa after the 520 C anneal, then rising to 160 MPa after the further 400 C anneal [obs1].
Panel F2a shows RT yield stress is strongly orientation dependent: ~9 MPa for [1 1 -2 1.85], ~148-165 MPa for [11-20], ~143 MPa for [01-10], and [0001] fractures at ~355 MPa without yielding [obs2].

Panel F2a shows that between RT and 400 C the alloy's [11-20]/[01-10] yield stress falls only from ~165 to ~105 MPa, whereas the pure-Mg reference falls sharply from ~270 to ~15 MPa and sits near 10 MPa in the soft orientations [obs3].
reference_reasoning.proposition: Nanoplate number density falls from 9.8 to 0.3 per um after the 520 C anneal and recovers to 9.0 per um after the further 400 C anneal [n9]; yield stress in [11-20] falls from 167 to 113 MPa after the same 520 C anneal and recovers to 160 MPa after the same further 400 C anneal [obs1]; the two quantities rise and fall together across all three treatments, while nanoplate thickness (28, then 84, then 14 nm) does not follow this up-down-up pattern [n9][obs1], so the strengthening tracks plate density rather than the heat-treatment step itself [writer inference], consistent with the orientation-dependent strength levels reported for [11-20] and [01-10] [n12].
reference_reasoning.assumption: The comparison assumes no other microstructural variable changed by the anneals (grain size, dislocation content) is independently driving the yield-stress swing, so that the density-yield correlation reflects plate density's role rather than a confound [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.open: It remains open by what mechanism the nanoplates raise yield stress (dislocation blocking, load transfer, or another size-dependent effect), since only density (not the accompanying thickness change) tracks the yield-stress pattern across the three treatments [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.handoff: The next step carries forward that yield strength in the alloy is tied to LPSO nanoplate density rather than to the anneal per se, alongside the magnitude finding that [11-20] and [01-10] reach ~145-165 MPa at RT, about 11x the pure-Mg single crystal [n12].

dependency.why: Without step 1's nanoplate density and thickness values across the three heat treatments, the yield-stress numbers in this step (167/113/160 MPa) have no feature-size series to compare against, so the tracking-versus-independent question cannot be answered.

combining.proposition: Yield stress tracks nanoplate number density across the three heat treatments: both fall after the 520 C anneal and both recover after the further 400 C anneal, so the strengthening follows plate density rather than the anneal itself.

observations: Panel F10a shows the tensile [0001] test at RT starting flow at ~72 MPa, serrated between ~52 and ~80 MPa, reaching ~45% plastic strain before fracture [obs1].
Panel F10b shows the tensile gauge filled with fine bands inclined to the [0001] tensile axis, across which the marked basal-plane trace kinks [obs2].
reference_reasoning.proposition: The same [0001] orientation that step 2 found could not yield in compression, fracturing at ~355 MPa, instead flows in tension at ~65-80 MPa out to ~45% plastic strain, a four- to five-fold stress asymmetry between the two loading senses that a single slip mechanism cannot produce, and the tension-side deformation proceeds instead by kink-band formation [n18].
reference_reasoning.assumption: The inference assumes the compression fracture stress from step 2 and the tensile flow stress measured here are directly comparable as two loading senses on the identical crystal orientation, and that the observed banding and basal-trace kinking in F10b, not slip, is what accommodates the ~45% tensile strain [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.open: It remains open whether kink-band formation also operates during the compressive loading that instead produced brittle fracture at ~355 MPa, or whether the compression path is blocked from kinking by some other constraint [writer inference].
reference_reasoning.handoff: The claim that [0001] elongates ~45% at 65-80 MPa by kink-band formation, the first bulk demonstration of tensile ductility by kinking, is carried forward as the mechanism established for this orientation [n18].

dependency.why: Without step 2's ~355 MPa compressive fracture stress for [0001] there is no basis for computing the tension/compression asymmetry or for concluding that slip alone cannot explain the behavior.

reasoning: The evidence begins with bright-field TEM at g=0002 showing strong planar fault-like contrast on (0001), at roughly ten plates per um [obs1].
HAADF-STEM resolves these plates as bright, heavy-atom-rich bands only a few atomic layers wide, with a 1 nm inset resolving a single such band [obs2].

This contrast and composition identify the dense basal planar defects as LPSO nanoplates, i.e. aggregates of four-layer Zn/Y-segregated fcc-type stacking faults rather than conventional stacking faults [n8].
TEM after the 520 C water quench shows only one thick dark plate, and the further 400 C anneal restores many thin plates [obs3].
Counting these plates across treatments gives a density/thickness sequence of 9.8 -> 0.3 -> 9.0 per um and mean thickness 28 -> 84 -> 14 nm for as-grown / 520 C / 520->400 C [obs4].

Together these establish that heat treatment sets nanoplate density and thickness: ~9.8 per um and ~28 nm as-grown, ~0.3 per um and ~84 nm after 520 C, ~9.0 per um and ~14 nm after the further 400 C anneal [n9].
Turning to mechanical response, yield stress in [11-20] at RT is measured as 167 MPa as-grown, 113 MPa after the 520 C anneal, and 160 MPa after the further 400 C anneal [obs1].

This tracks the density/thickness sequence from step 1: yield stress drops when nanoplate density falls and thickness rises (520 C), then recovers when density is restored and thickness falls again (further 400 C anneal), matching the pattern in [n9] [writer inference].
RT yield stress is also reported by orientation: ~9 MPa for [1 1 -2 1.85], ~148-165 MPa for [11-20], ~143 MPa for [01-10], and [0001] fracturing at ~355 MPa without yielding [obs2].

Between RT and 400 C the alloy's [11-20]/[01-10] yield stress falls only from ~165 to ~105 MPa, while a pure-Mg reference falls from ~270 to ~15 MPa and sits near 10 MPa in the soft orientations, showing the alloy retains its strength advantage where pure Mg does not [obs3].
Taken together, this establishes that yield stress is strongly orientation dependent and, in [11-20] and [01-10], reaches ~145-165 MPa at RT, about 11x the pure-Mg single crystal [n12].

For the [0001] orientation specifically, a tensile RT test shows flow stress starting at ~72 MPa, serrated between ~52 and ~80 MPa, with the specimen reaching ~45% plastic strain before fracture [obs1].
The tensile gauge is filled with fine bands inclined to the [0001] tensile direction, across which the marked basal-plane trace kinks [obs2].

Comparing this ~65-80 MPa tensile stress range to the [0001] behavior noted in step 2 (fracture at ~355 MPa without yielding under a different loading path) shows that under tension the crystal instead deforms plastically at a much lower stress via kink-band formation [writer inference].
This establishes that in tension along [0001] the crystal elongates ~45% at 65-80 MPa by kink-band formation, the first bulk demonstration of tensile ductility by kinking [n18].
end_to_end.why_weakest: the heat-treatment yield-stress sequence tracks nanoplate density/thickness fairly well, but the orientation data in the same step show yield stress swinging from ~9 MPa to ~355 MPa in a single alloy with presumably the same nanoplates, so the claim that the feature size measured in step 1 is what carries the strength is confounded by an orientation effect the evidence doesn't disentangle.
